The thing with rimfires is that most fixed objective centerfire scopes are set to be parallax free at 100 yards. Because of the way optics work, you aren't going to pick up much parallax at ranges longer than that either. 100 yards is a pretty long shot for a .22lr, maybe not .22 mag.

If you are shooting at typical rimfire ranges like 25 or 50 yards, parallax might be an issue with those fixed objective centerfire scopes. This is why fixed objective rimfires have a shorter parallax setting (typically 50 yards). This is also why I bought an adjustable objective rimfire scope.

Rimfire scopes are parallax-adjusted at 50 yards. Centerfire scopes are adjusted for use at longer ranges.

The adjustment is important - if you have the dollars, you can get a scope with adjustable parallax and dial it in to the range of your shot. It matters because, if the adjustment is not correct, your eye must be perfectly centered behind the scope. Any deviation from that, and an unadjusted scope will give you a false point of aim. If the parallax is dialed in correctly, however, then your point of aim is always correct.

Of course you still have to account for bullet drop, too.
